clue.text: Jenny kissed him

parts.note: recalls the famous short poem beginning 'Jenny kiss'd me when we met', written by a Romantic essayist and poet about Jane Welsh Carlyle

explanation.surface: A gossip item about whom Jenny gave a kiss.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem 'Rondeau' (Jenny kiss'd me) is by the essayist and poet James Henry Leigh Hunt; the 'him' is its speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet who wrote of being kissed by Jenny is the person the clue points to.

clue.text: Loaf cut up for tea?

parts.note: sugar used to come in a large cone called a loaf, which was broken into pieces to sweeten tea

explanation.surface: Slicing up bread for an afternoon meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaf' reads as bread, but it is a sugarloaf, the cone sugar was once sold in.
explanation.definitionFit: Cubes of sweetener dropped into a cup were once cut from a solid sugarloaf.

clue.text: Children-one's a little girl

parts.note: one is I, and 's stands for is, so one's gives I followed by S
Sue is a girl's name, short for Susan

explanation.surface: Of the kids, one is a little girl.
explanation.walkthrough: Sue is a short form of Susan, hence 'little'.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue is a legal term for a person's offspring.

clue.text: Capital wrinkle for daily use?

parts.note: a top or head (capital) plus a line (wrinkle), as printed in big letters across a daily newspaper

explanation.surface: A clever tip from the city for everyday life.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital means top or head, and in large capital letters; a wrinkle is a line; 'daily' is a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: The bold title over a newspaper story combines a top and a printed line.

clue.text: Awkward in gun-laying-no end of bungling

indicators.note: bungling suggests the remaining letters are botched into a new order
no end means the last letter of the hyphenated word is dropped

explanation.surface: Clumsy work in aiming a gun, with constant bungling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end' drops the final G of GUNLAYING, and 'bungling' rearranges UNLAYING.
explanation.definitionFit: Ungainly means clumsy and lacking grace.

clue.text: Lots of soldiers, mounted — inferior, in a way

indicators.note: mounted means going up, which in a down clue reverses the letters
in means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: St is short for street, a way
poor means inferior

explanation.surface: Cavalry soldiers riding along a low-quality road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts POOR inside ST, making SPOORT, and 'mounted' turns it upwards to give TROOPS. 'Mounted' suggests cavalry.
explanation.definitionFit: Troops are soldiers in numbers, a body of armed forces.

clue.text: Mocking old Greek who returns money order

indicators.note: returns tells us the run of money and order is read backwards

parts.note: a sum is an amount of money
OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek scoffer sends back a postal money order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' turns SUM + OM, giving MOMUS. A money order is a postal payment slip, which the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: Momus was the Greek god of satire and ridicule, a figure of mockery in old myth.

clue.text: Indian driver whose charge was very big

definitions.text: Indian driver whose charge was very big

parts.words: Indian driver whose charge was very big
parts.note: the driver steers not a car but an elephant, a very large charge in the Indian subcontinent

explanation.surface: A driver in India with a huge fare to collect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charge' looks like a fee or a passenger, but it is the animal in his care.
explanation.definitionFit: A mahout rides and steers an elephant, the huge animal in his keeping.

clue.text: Play, when rough, alarmed MO

indicators.note: when rough hints the letters given are roughed up into a new order

explanation.surface: A medical officer gets alarmed when the play turns rough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when rough' rearranges ALARMED + MO. MO is a Medical Officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A melodrama is a stage drama of exaggerated sensational plot.

clue.text: Being sober, remained in hearing

indicators.note: in hearing means the word is judged by how it is said

parts.note: stayed means remained

explanation.surface: A witness stayed sober throughout a court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hearing' looks like a court session but signals sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Staid describes someone serious and respectable, sedate rather than lively.

clue.text: Has to break the nag-a wild one

parts.note: must means has to

indicators.note: break suggests smashing up the letters of the next word, as well as taming a horse

explanation.surface: Someone must tame the nag, a wild horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break' rearranges NAG into ANG, after MUST. 'Break' in the surface is horse training, which fits the wild horse answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A mustang is a feral horse of the American plains, the wild sort of nag.

clue.text: Hamlet's character shown in work by Holyhead essayist

parts.note: op is short for opus, a musical work
read as holy head: the head of holy is H
Elia was the pen name of the essayist Charles Lamb

explanation.surface: A role from Hamlet appears in a piece by a writer from the Welsh port of Holyhead.
explanation.walkthrough: Holyhead, a port in Anglesey, Wales, splits as 'holy head', giving the first letter of holy. 'Hamlet's character' is a character in Shakespeare's play.
explanation.definitionFit: Ophelia is the young woman Hamlet loves in Shakespeare's tragedy, one of its main roles.

clue.text: Big-wig appears to be affected by inflation

definitions.meaning: an important or fashionable person, a toff

definitions.text: appears to be affected by inflation
definitions.meaning: grows larger as if pumped up with air

explanation.definitionFit: A swell is an old word for a grand personage, and to puff up from inflation is to bulge outwards.

clue.text: Confiscated money carried by half-back

indicators.note: carried by means one piece is held inside the other
back means the word for half is read backwards

parts.note: demi- means half
a pound is a unit of money

explanation.surface: A half-back on a football team has their money taken away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns DEMI into IMED, and 'carried by' places POUND inside it. Half-back is a football position, the surface's disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: To impound goods is to seize them by law, so impounded means seized.

clue.text: Possibly PGs learn to help boarders?

indicators.note: possibly hints that the letters given could be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: Paying guests might learn how to look after lodgers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges PGS + LEARN. PGs are paying guests, so 'boarders' looks like lodgers, but it means sailors boarding an enemy ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Grappling irons were thrown to hook an enemy vessel so that a boarding party could cross.

clue.text: Main stop in Alaska ?

definitions.meaning: a place where a ship stops at sea, the main being the ocean
the largest city of the US state of Alaska

explanation.definitionFit: A berth where vessels drop their hooks shares its name with Alaska's largest city.

clue.text: Report gold missing from .Welsh town

indicators.note: missing from means one piece is taken out of the other

parts.note: Bangor is a town in north Wales
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A news report on gold going missing in a Welsh town.
explanation.walkthrough: Bangor is a cathedral city in north Wales. 'Report' is a loud noise, not a news story.
explanation.definitionFit: A report can be the sharp noise of a gun firing, which is a loud explosive sound.

clue.text: First of general tendencies picked up by field workers

indicators.note: first of means take the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: leanings are tendencies

explanation.surface: A general's first tendencies were noticed by staff in the field.
explanation.walkthrough: Gleaners picked up leftover grain from fields after harvest.
explanation.definitionFit: Gleanings are the stray ears of grain gathered from a reaped field.

clue.text: Rough week for dance centre in Derbyshire

indicators.note: centre means one piece is placed at the heart of the other

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance

indicators.note: rough suggests the letters given are disordered

explanation.surface: A rough week at a dance centre in an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rough' turns WEEK into KEWE, and 'centre' places it inside BALL. Bakewell is a market town in Derbyshire, an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: Bakewell is a small town in the Peak District, in the county named.

clue.text: Interval for music arising daily, one concludes

indicators.note: arising means going up, which in a down clue reverses the word

parts.note: The Times is a daily newspaper
taken as written

explanation.surface: A musical gap appears each day, as one finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arising' turns TIMES upward to SEMIT, and 'one' ends it ('concludes'). The setter's own paper is the daily.
explanation.definitionFit: A semitone is the smallest interval in Western music, half a whole step.

clue.text: Sweet music ?

definitions.meaning: a hard stick of candy sold at British seaside resorts
a genre of loud guitar-led popular music

explanation.definitionFit: Seaside candy sticks and guitar-based pop share one name, a confection and a musical style.

clue.text: Club 'estimate appears steep

parts.note: a mace is a heavy club
to rate is to estimate

explanation.surface: A club's assessment says the slope is steep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'steep' is a verb, to soak, not a slope.
explanation.definitionFit: To soften something by soaking it in liquid is to steep it.

clue.text: Main element in fifty paste ingredients

indicators.note: in means one piece goes inside the other
ingredients suggests the letters given are mixed together

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: The principal element in fifty batches of paste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ingredients' rearranges PASTE, and 'in' puts L inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A staple is a chief commodity or basic item, a principal component.

clue.text: Fresh fellow from Crawley ?

parts.note: raw means fresh, uncooked
a don is a university fellow

explanation.surface: A new man arrives from the West Sussex town of Crawley.
explanation.walkthrough: Crawley looks like the Sussex town, but it is Rawdon Crawley, a character in Thackeray's novel Vanity Fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Rawdon is the first name of Becky Sharp's husband in the Thackeray novel.

clue.text: Lying words about return of confectionery

indicators.note: about means one piece goes round the other

parts.note: prose is ordinary written words

indicators.note: return of means the sweet's word is read backwards

parts.note: a tart is a pastry confection

explanation.surface: Fibbing talk about sweets being sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return of' turns TART into TRAT, and 'about' wraps PROSE around it. 'Lying' means lying flat, not telling fibs.
explanation.definitionFit: Prostrate means lying face down, stretched out flat on the ground.

clue.text: Bookmaker's attendants ?

definitions.meaning: the leaves that go to make up a book, read as what a book is made of
young servants or boys who wait on a noble

explanation.definitionFit: Leaves that compose a book and boys serving a lord share one word.

clue.text: Playwright cribs entire part?

indicators.note: part means the answer is a section of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Does a dramatist copy a whole role?
explanation.walkthrough: Cribs here means copies, as in cheating.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen was the Norwegian dramatist of A Doll's House.

clue.text: .Not the " piece of cake drivers appreciate

definitions.text: Not the " piece of cake drivers appreciate

parts.words: Not the " piece of cake drivers appreciate
parts.note: a portion of cake, but also a golf shot curving off line, which golfers with drivers dislike

explanation.surface: A treat that motorists do not enjoy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drivers' reads as motorists but means golfers using the long club.
explanation.definitionFit: A slice is both a wedge of cake and a golf shot that curves away to the side.

clue.text: Key made grating sound, it's understood

parts.note: G is a musical key
rasped means made a harsh grating noise

explanation.surface: A turned key gives a harsh noise; the point is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: To grasp an idea is to understand it.

clue.text: This feeling could be mine too

indicators.note: could be hints the letters given might be reshaped into another word

explanation.surface: Someone says they might share the same feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges MINE + TOO.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotion is a feeling such as joy or grief.

clue.text: European underground

definitions.meaning: a root vegetable grown in the soil, like a turnip

explanation.definitionFit: A Scandinavian national and a buried root crop share one name.

clue.text: Sculptor appears on knees making collection — about £2

indicators.note: about means one piece goes round the other
making collection hints that the letters given are gathered up anew

parts.note: L stands for pound (libra), so two pounds is LL

explanation.surface: A sculptor on their knees takes up a collection of about two pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making collection' rearranges ON KNEES into NOEKENS, and 'about' puts it round LL. Joseph Nollekens was an 18th-century English sculptor.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Nollekens was a celebrated Georgian sculptor of portrait busts.
